title: The four phrases
hookLine: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease

lines: BACK TO THE FIRST WORD: METTA.
cards: In Buddhist teaching, loving-kindness isn't only a feeling you wait for. People practice it on purpose, with words, again and again, the way you'd practice a scale on a piano.
Metta was the first word on this path, on day one, before any of the stories. Back then it was a word. Now it gets hands and feet.
Camp three, the practices, begins here, and for the next sixty days the path is about doing: the sitting, the walking, the precepts, the giving, the chanting, the holy days. And it starts with metta.

teach.b: Here are the four phrases this path uses, in a common modern form. May you be safe. May you be happy.
May you be healthy. May you live with ease. Each one is a wish, not a demand.
Safe: free from danger, inside and out. Happy: a settled gladness, not a party. Healthy: in body and mind.
At ease: life not being a constant struggle. Now, an honest note.
These exact four lines are modern, and teachers word them a little differently.
What's old is the wish itself. The Metta Sutta, a text Theravada Buddhists chant, wishes that all beings be happy and secure, that their hearts be glad.
The Path of Purification, an old manual by the monk Buddhaghosa, gives phrases of its own.
So the phrases are a tool, like a handrail: something for the mind to lean on when the feeling isn't there yet. And that's the part people find surprising: you don't have to feel warm to begin.
You say the words slowly and sincerely, and you notice what happens. Some days, warmth.
Some days, nothing. Some days, resistance. All of it counts.
Over the next ten days you'll send these wishes out in widening circles: to yourself, a helper, a friend, a stranger, a difficult person, and finally everyone. Today, just the four lines.

how: One way Buddhists practice metta is by repeating short wishes, silently or aloud, for themselves and others; the wording varies by teacher and school, and Theravada communities often chant the Metta Sutta itself.

o: romantic love for one special person
loving-kindness, a wish for others' good
a calm, empty mind, free of all thought

games.q: what's inside each phrase — tap the pairs.
p: free from danger, inside and out

s: these exact four phrases come word for word from the Buddha
the wording is modern; the wish is old, as in the Metta Sutta.
you have to feel warm before metta practice works
the phrases are a handrail: you begin sincerely and notice what happens.
the Metta Sutta wishes that all beings be happy and secure
it's a short text that Theravada Buddhists chant.

games.q: you say the four phrases and feel nothing at all. what does the practice say?
games.why: warmth, nothing and resistance all count. the phrases are something to lean on until the feeling comes.

practice: Silently and slowly, say the four phrases once, with a pause and a breath after each: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease.
Don't aim them at anyone yet; just notice what they do in the body, softening, nothing, a little resistance, and whatever shows up is fine. When the words are done, rest in the quiet after them.

wordCard.voice: Metta. Loving-kindness: the old practice behind the four phrases, may you be safe, happy, healthy, and at ease.

carryVoice: Your line: may you be at ease. The last of the four phrases, and the one to keep. Ninety-seven days, and counting.
